key_terms.meaning: Kernel structure that describes one process: its PID, state, stack pointer, memory map, open files and links to parent and children.
All task_structs held in linked lists and hash tables, so the kernel can find a task by PID or walk the parent-child tree.
Positive integer that names a task; PID 1 is init, and the kernel reuses numbers after a wrap.
Hardware event that makes the CPU save its context and jump to a handler; identified by an IRQ line and a vector number.
Asynchronous notification sent to a process (SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGCHLD) with a default action and an optional handler.
Counter of timer ticks since boot; one tick lasts 1/HZ seconds, where HZ is a build-time constant.
Address a program uses; the MMU translates it through page tables into a physical frame address.
Exception raised when a virtual page has no valid mapping; the kernel handler either builds the mapping or kills the process.
Busy-wait lock; the holder must not sleep, so it suits short critical sections shared with interrupt handlers.
Sleeping lock with a counter; down() blocks when the count is zero and up() wakes a waiter.
List of sleeping tasks protected by a lock; wake_up() moves them to the run queue, used by the wait_event macros.
Kernel byte buffer with a read end and a write end, carrying one-way data between related processes.
Kernel endpoint for two-way communication, named by a file descriptor and, for inet sockets, by an IP address and port.
System call by which one process (the tracer) stops, reads and writes the registers and memory of another (the tracee).
Object holding a file's metadata: type, mode, owner, size, timestamps and block pointers, plus operation tables in the VFS.
Virtual File System switch: one inode, dentry, file and superblock interface, so every file system looks the same to system calls.
Number in a device file that selects which driver handles the device.
Number in a device file that selects which instance (disk, partition, tty) the driver should serve.
Table of function pointers (open, read, write, ioctl, release) that a driver fills so file operations reach device code.
Data with one copy per CPU, read and written without locking because only the local CPU touches its copy.

takeaways: Every running program is one task_struct, and the process table is the set of lists that finds it by PID or by parent.
Interrupts travel from hardware to the kernel, signals travel from the kernel to a process; both arrive without warning.
The timer tick keeps time, expires timeouts, and gives the scheduler its regular chance to switch tasks.
A process only ever sees virtual addresses; Linux fills in the translation map lazily, page by page, as faults arrive.
Kernel data is shared between CPUs and interrupt handlers, so each critical section needs a lock chosen to match that context.
Pipes and sockets are kernel buffers reached through file descriptors, and ptrace is a kernel channel for one process to control another.
The VFS inode and its operation tables make ext2 on disk and /proc in memory answer the same read() call.
A device is a major number, a minor number and a file_operations table.
Multiprocessor Linux buys correctness with locking and speed with per-CPU data plus a load balancer.
bank_note: Long answers here almost always ask you to trace one event — a kill, a page fault, a read() on a device — through the kernel structures it touches, so name each structure, the field used and the step in order.

bank.q: Draw a task_struct and label the fields used for lookup: pid, state, parent and children links, mm and files. Explain how the process table finds a task by PID and how it lists that task's children.
outline: task_struct is the process descriptor, allocated in kernel memory
pid field plus the PID hash table gives O(1) lookup
parent and children/sibling links form the process tree
state field values: running, interruptible, stopped, zombie
mm holds the address space, files holds the open file table

bank.q: Explain how a hardware interrupt reaches its handler: the inter-request line, the vector, saving the context and returning. Say why Linux splits handling into a top half and a bottom half, with one example of each.
outline: device raises IRQ, interrupt controller signals the CPU
CPU reads the vector and indexes the interrupt descriptor table
current context saved on the kernel stack, interrupts disabled on that CPU
top half runs quickly: acknowledge device, copy urgent data
bottom half (softirq, tasklet, workqueue) does the long work with interrupts on
return path restores context, possibly reschedules

bank.q: Define a signal. List four common signals with their default actions, and describe how a pending signal is delivered and what happens after a handler returns.
outline: signal is an asynchronous notification, numbered 1 to 64
SIGTERM terminates, SIGKILL terminates and cannot be caught, SIGCHLD notifies parent, SIGSEGV core dumps
pending bit set on the task, blocked by the signal mask
delivered when the process returns from kernel to user mode
handler runs on the user stack, then sigreturn restores the old context
default action taken if no handler is installed

bank.q: Explain address translation in Linux: virtual address, page, page frame, page table and TLB. Then give the steps of handling a page fault on a valid but not yet mapped page.
outline: virtual address splits into page number and offset
page table maps page number to frame number plus permission bits
TLB caches recent translations
fault traps to kernel, faulting address read from a control register
handler checks the VMA for the address
valid: read from disk or zero-fill a frame, install mapping, return and retry the instruction
invalid: send SIGSEGV

bank.q: Compare spinlocks, kernel semaphores and wait queues. For each, state whether the holder may sleep and where the kernel uses it.
outline: spinlock busy-waits, non-preemptible section, holder must not sleep
used for short sections shared with interrupt handlers
semaphore counts, down() sleeps the caller, used for longer holds
mutex is a semaphore with count one and an owner
wait queue holds sleeping tasks until a condition becomes true
wake_up moves tasks to the run queue
rule: never sleep inside interrupt context

bank.q: Describe byte-stream pipes: how one is created, the read and write ends, what read() returns at end-of-file, and why the pipe has a fixed capacity.
outline: pipe() returns two file descriptors
anonymous pipe exists only through these descriptors
writer blocks when the buffer is full, reader blocks when empty
read() returns 0 when all write ends are closed
SIGPIPE if the reader has gone
fixed capacity keeps memory bounded and gives natural flow control

bank.q: A user program calls read() on the device file of a character driver. Trace the call from the system call entry to the copy of bytes into user memory. State where the major number, the minor number and the file_operations table are used.
outline: syscall entry, arguments checked, file descriptor looked up in the file table
file points to a dentry and inode; inode type says character device
major number selects the driver through the character device table
minor number is passed to the driver to pick the instance
VFS calls the read entry of the driver's file_operations
driver copies data with copy_to_user and returns the count
return value and errors handled at the syscall exit

bank.q: Two CPUs increment the same kernel counter without protection and one update is lost. Show how the race happens, then remove it once with an atomic operation and once with a spinlock. Explain why a semaphore is the wrong choice when the code also runs in an interrupt handler.
outline: read-modify-write is not one instruction at the memory bus level
interleaving of load and store loses an update
atomic_t or atomic_inc uses a single locked instruction
spinlock gives mutual exclusion around a longer section
spin_lock_irqsave also disables local interrupts to avoid deadlock
a semaphore may sleep, and sleeping is illegal in interrupt context
keep the critical section short to limit contention

bank.q: Trace the shell command kill -TERM <pid> from the kill system call to the target process running its handler. Cover PID lookup, the permission check, the pending bit, waking a sleeping task and delivery on return to user mode.
outline: kill() enters the kernel with a PID and a signal number
process table lookup by PID fails with ESRCH if absent
permission check: same user or a privileged process
signal bit set in the pending set of the target
if the target sleeps interruptibly it is woken
signal delivered at the next return to user mode
handler installed by the process runs, else the default action

bank.q: A process touches a heap address it has never used before. Trace the event from the instruction to every possible outcome, including the case where the process is killed.
outline: MMU finds no valid translation and raises a page fault
faulting address and error code passed to the handler
kernel searches the VMAs of the task for the address
inside a VMA: allocate a zeroed frame, insert the mapping
page table updated, TLB flushed if needed
instruction restarted and now succeeds
outside every VMA: SIGSEGV delivered
under memory pressure: reclaim or OOM kill

bank.q: Analyse demand paging with lazy allocation in Linux. What does the kernel save, what does each fault cost, and how can overcommit end in the OOM killer?
outline: pages are mapped only when first touched
saves memory and start-up time for large sparse programs
each fault costs a trap, a frame allocation and often disk I/O
overcommit allows total virtual size to exceed RAM plus swap
reclaim, swap and page cache shrink under pressure
when reclaim fails the OOM killer picks a task
tuning knobs change how strict overcommit is

bank.q: Explain how a debugger uses ptrace to set a breakpoint and read a register of the program under test. Then analyse why ptrace is treated as a security-sensitive interface.
outline: tracer attaches with PTRACE_ATTACH or starts the child with PTRACE_TRACEME
tracee stops at each signal and syscall boundary
tracer writes a trap instruction over the target byte
SIGTRAP returns control to the tracer, original byte restored
PTRACE_PEEK/POKE read and write memory, GETREGS reads registers
a tracing process can read and change another process's memory
hence the same-user rule and restrictions on setuid programs

bank.q: Compare the on-disk inode of ext2 with the in-memory inode of the VFS. Evaluate how the operation tables in the in-memory inode let /proc answer the same read() call as a file on disk.
outline: on-disk inode holds mode, owner, size, times, direct and indirect block pointers
no function pointers on disk, fixed layout
VFS inode built in memory when the file is first touched
inode_operations and file_operations hold function pointers
address space operations connect the page cache to the backing store
ext2 read goes through the block device; proc read builds text
uniform interface: the system call never knows which file system it hit

bank.q: Linux once serialised kernel code with one global lock and now runs it on many CPUs at once. Evaluate the change: per-CPU data, spinlocks, cache behaviour on contended locks, and the job of the load balancer.
outline: global lock gave correctness but no scaling
per-CPU data removes sharing for counters and caches
spinlock protects genuinely shared state, cost rises with contention
cache line bouncing makes a hot lock expensive
lock ordering rules prevent deadlock
load balancer moves runnable tasks between CPUs
affinity and NUMA placement affect performance
trade-off: fine-grained locking is harder to get right

glossary.def: The task_struct in kernel memory that holds everything the kernel knows about one process.
The lists and hash tables that hold all process descriptors and allow lookup by PID or by parent.
The first user process, always PID 1, which starts the rest of the system.
A finished process whose descriptor stays until its parent collects the exit status.
Interrupt descriptor table; holds the handler entry point for each interrupt vector.
The interrupt handler that runs immediately with interrupts partly disabled and must be short.
Deferred interrupt work done later, as a softirq, tasklet or workqueue, with interrupts enabled.
User function that runs instead of a signal's default action when the process has installed one.
Build-time constant giving timer ticks per second; jiffies counts those ticks.
Memory management unit; hardware that translates virtual addresses to physical addresses using page tables.
Fixed-size block of virtual memory, commonly 4 KiB on x86.
Fixed-size block of physical memory that holds one page.
Per-process table that maps page numbers to frame numbers and holds permission bits.
Translation lookaside buffer; a small cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Loading a page into memory only when it is first touched, not when it is mapped.
Code that touches shared data and must run as if it were alone.
An operation that completes as one indivisible step, so no other CPU sees a half-done result.
Sleeping lock with a single owner, used when the critical section may block.
Named pipe; a pipe that has a path in the file system so unrelated processes can open it.
Socket that stays inside one machine and is addressed by a file-system path.
Directory entry object that links a file name to its inode and caches path lookups.
In-memory object describing one mounted file system.
Device read and written as a stream of bytes, such as a terminal or serial port.
System call that passes device-specific commands and arguments straight to a driver.
Scheduler activity that moves runnable tasks to idle CPUs to keep every CPU busy.
